payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: In the edited image, is the woman's jacket fully closed, with its front panels together and no visible opening remaining along the closure?
node.criteria: Pass: the jacket is visibly fully closed, with its front panels together and no opening along the closure. Fail: the jacket is visibly not fully closed, including any visible opening along the closure. Unknown: the closure or its full extent cannot be judged from the image.
node.binding: Directly inspect the requested endpoint in the edited image; the input image is context for identifying the woman's jacket, not a prerequisite for checking the endpoint.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows the woman's jacket hanging open, with a clear gap between the front panels.
The edited image shows the jacket hanging open, with a clear gap between its front panels.
The jacket is visibly open in the edited image, with its front panels separated and a large opening remaining.

fulfillment: The node’s repeated, high-confidence “no” judgments conflict with the supplied aggregate reference, but the visible edited image appears to show the woman turned sideways with the bright pink jacket hanging open and its front panels separated; the source also appears open. This is substantive visual disagreement, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure: all five executions are valid, queried, and eligible, and both supports were evaluated. Do not flip the label merely to match the reference. Investigate whether the target binding identifies the correct garment/person and whether the closure criterion is being applied to the visible jacket rather than obscured or ambiguous regions. Keep endpoint completion distinct from comparative progress: a clearly fully closed jacket supports completion; if it is not fully closed, compare source and edit for actual closure progress, and reserve “no” for no progress, “partial” for visible progress, and “unknown” when evidence is insufficient. The current traces repeatedly assert no progress without describing a concrete source-to-edit comparison, so require evidence tied to observable panel alignment/opening in both images and calibrate confidence to visibility and pose. Preserve the original rubric and required checks; the reference label constrains the aggregate but is not atomic ground truth.
s2: The node’s binding and comparison are too vague for this case: the woman changes pose substantially, and the edited jacket swings outward, so “still open” does not establish that no closure progress occurred. Keep the same woman and pink jacket anchored across both images, and require a direct comparison of visible closure cues (front-panel separation, overlap/alignment, and any visible fastening) while accounting for pose and occlusion. Distinguish “not fully closed” from “no progress”: the edited image can remain open yet show partial progress; use unknown if the changed pose or occlusion prevents a reliable comparison. The traces repeatedly give high-confidence fail judgments without concrete paired evidence, so calibrate confidence to what is actually visible and state the source-versus-edit cues supporting the status. Preserve the completion and partial-progress criteria; do not force the reference label. This is a visual-evidence/binding issue, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure.
